section.heading: 2.5 Matrix Factorizations
section.paragraph: A factorization of a matrix $$A$$ is an equation that expresses $$A$$ as a product of two or more matrices. Whereas matrix multiplication involves a synthesis of data (combining the effects of two or more linear transformations into a single matrix), matrix factorization is an analysis of data. In the language of computer science, the expression of $$A$$ as a product amounts to a preprocessing of the data in $$A,$$ organizing that data into two or more parts whose structures are more useful in some way, perhaps more accessible for computation.

Matrix factorizations and, later, factorizations of linear transformations will appear at a number of key points throughout the text. This section focuses on a factorization that lies at the heart of several important computer programs widely used in applications, such as the airflow problem described in the chapter introduction. Several other factorizations, to be studied later, are introduced in the exercises.
section.heading: The LU Factorization
section.paragraph: The $$LU$$ factorization, described below, is motivated by the fairly common industrial and business problem of solving a sequence of equations, all with the same coefficient matrix:
$$A \textbf{x} = \textbf{b}_{1} , A \textbf{x} = \textbf{b}_{2} , \ldots , A \textbf{x} = \textbf{b}_{p}$$
See Exercise 32, for example. Also see Section 5.8, where the inverse power method is used to estimate eigenvalues of a matrix by solving equations like those in sequence (1), one at a time.

When $$A$$ is invertible, one could compute $$A^{- 1}$$ and then compute $$A^{- 1}\textbf{b}_{1}$$ , $$A^{- 1}\textbf{b}_{2}$$ , and so on. However, it is more efficient to solve the first equation in sequence (1) by row reduction and obtain an $$LU$$ factorization of $$A$$ at the same time. Thereafter, the remaining equations in sequence (1) are solved with the $$LU$$ factorization.

At first, assume that $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix that can be row reduced to echelon form, without row interchanges. (Later, we will treat the general case.) Then $$A$$ can be written in the form $$A = LU$$ , where $$L$$ is an $$m \times m$$ lower triangular matrix with $$1 \text{’s}$$ on the diagonal and $$U$$ is an $$m \times n$$ echelon form of $$A$$ For instance, see Figure 1. Such a factorization is called an LU factorization of $$A$$ The matrix $$L$$ is invertible and is called a unit lower triangular matrix.

image.alt: A figure shows the multiplication of a 4 by 4 upper triangular matrix and a 4 by 5 lower triangular matrix.

section.paragraph: Before studying how to construct $$L$$ and $$U$$ , we should look at why they are so useful. When $$A = LU$$ , the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ can be written as $$L(U\textbf{x}) = \textbf{b}$$ . Writing $$\textbf{y}$$ for $$U\textbf{x}$$ , we can find $$\textbf{x}$$ by solving the pair of equations
$$\boxed{L \mathbf{y} & = & b U \mathbf{x} & = & y}$$

First solve $$L\textbf{y} = \textbf{b}$$ for $$\textbf{y}$$ , and then solve $$U\textbf{x} = \textbf{y}$$ for $$\mathbf{x}$$ . See Figure 2. Each equation is easy to solve because $$L$$ and $$U$$ are triangular.

image.alt: A figure shows three parallelograms each with a point labeled x, y, and b respectively. The arrows between them indicate the multiplication process.

figure.caption: Figure 2 Factorization of the mapping x↦Ax

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Use this $$LU$$ factorization of $$A$$ to solve $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ , where $$\mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 9} \\ 5 \\ 7 \\ 11 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The solution of $$L\textbf{y} = \textbf{b}$$ needs only $$6$$ multiplications and $$6$$ additions, because the arithmetic takes place only in column $$5$$ . (The zeros below each pivot in $$L$$ are created automatically by the choice of row operations.)

Then, for $$U\textbf{x} = \textbf{y}$$ , the “backward” phase of row reduction requires $$4$$ divisions, $$6$$ multiplications, and $$6$$ additions. (For instance, creating the zeros in column $$4$$ of $$\begin{bmatrix} U & \textbf{y} \end{bmatrix}$$ requires $$1$$ division in row $$4$$ and $$3$$ multiplication–addition pairs to add multiples of row $$4$$ to the rows above.)

To find $$\textbf{x}$$ requires $$28$$ arithmetic operations, or “flops” (floating point operations), excluding the cost of finding $$L$$ and $$U$$ . In contrast, row reduction of $$\begin{bmatrix} A & \textbf{b} \end{bmatrix}$$ to $$\begin{bmatrix} I & \textbf{x} \end{bmatrix}$$ takes $$62$$ operations.

section.paragraph: The computational efficiency of the $$LU$$ factorization depends on knowing $$L$$ and $$U$$ The next algorithm shows that the row reduction of $$A$$ to an echelon form $$U$$ amounts to an $$LU$$ factorization because it produces $$L$$ with essentially no extra work. After the first row reduction, $$L$$ and $$U$$ are available for solving additional equations whose coefficient matrix is $$A$$ .﻿
section.heading: An LU Factorization Algorithm
section.paragraph: Suppose $$A$$ can be reduced to an echelon form $$U$$ using only row replacements that add a multiple of one row to another row below it. In this case, there exist unit lower triangular elementary matrices $$E_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$E_{p}$$ , such that
$$E_{p} \hdots E_{1} A = U$$
Then
$$A = \left(\right. E_{p} \hdots E_{1} \left.\right)^{- 1} U = L U$$
where
$$L = \left(\right. E_{p} \hdots E_{1} \left.\right)^{- 1}$$
It can be shown that products and inverses of unit lower triangular matrices are also unit lower triangular. (For instance, see Exercise 19.) Thus $$L$$ is unit lower triangular.

Note that the row operations in equation (3), which reduce $$A$$ to $$U$$ , also reduce the $$L$$ in equation (4) to $$I$$ , because $$E_{p}\cdots E_{1}L = (E_{p}\cdots E_{1})(E_{p}\cdots E_{1})^{- 1} = I$$ . This observation is the key to constructing $$L$$ .

list.item: Reduce $$A$$ to an echelon form $$U$$ by a sequence of row replacement operations, if possible.
Place entries in $$L$$ such that the same sequence of row operations reduces $$L$$ to $$I$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Step 1 is not always possible, but when it is, the argument above shows that an $$LU$$ factorization exists. Example 2 will show how to implement step 2. By construction, $$L$$ will satisfy
$$\left(\right. E_{p} \hdots E_{1} \left.\right) L = I$$

using the same $$E_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$E_{p}$$ , as in equation (3). Thus $$L$$ will be invertible, by the Invertible Matrix Theorem, with $$(E_{p}\cdots E_{1}) = L^{- 1}$$ . From (3), $$L^{- 1}A = U$$ , and $$A = LU$$ . So step 2 will produce an acceptable $$L$$ .﻿

Solution
example.paragraph: Since $$A$$ has four rows, $$L$$ should be $$4 \times 4$$ . The first column of $$L$$ is the first column of $$A$$ divided by the top pivot entry:

To make this same correspondence of row operations on $$A$$ hold for the rest of $$L,$$ watch a row reduction of $$A$$ to an echelon form $$U$$ . That is, highlight the entries in each matrix that are used to determine the sequence of row operations that transform $$A$$ into $$U$$ . [See the highlighted entries in equation (5).]

section.paragraph: In practical work, row interchanges are nearly always needed, because partial pivoting is used for high accuracy. (Recall that this procedure selects, among the possible choices for a pivot, an entry in the column having the largest absolute value.) To handle row interchanges, the $$LU$$ factorization above can be modified easily to produce an $$L$$ that is permuted lower triangular, in the sense that a rearrangement (called a permutation) of the rows of $$L$$ can make $$L \left( \text{u} \text{n} \text{i} \text{t} \right)$$ lower triangular. The resulting permuted $$\mathbf{LU}$$ factorization solves $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ in the same way as before, except that the reduction of $$\begin{bmatrix} L & \textbf{b} \end{bmatrix}$$ to $$\begin{bmatrix} I & \textbf{y} \end{bmatrix}$$ follows the order of the pivots in $$L$$ from left to right, starting with the pivot in the first column. A reference to an “ $$LU$$ factorization” usually includes the possibility that $$L$$ might be permuted lower triangular. For details, see the Study Guide.

note.paragraph: STUDY GUIDE offers information about permuted $$LU$$ factorizations.

note.title: Numerical Notes
note.heading: Numerical Notes
note.paragraph: The following operation counts apply to an $$n \times n$$ dense matrix $$A$$ (with most entries nonzero) for $$n$$ moderately large, say, $$n \geq 30$$ .1﻿

list.item: Computing an $$LU$$ factorization of $$A$$ takes about $$2n^{3}/3$$ flops (about the same as row reducing $$\left. \begin{bmatrix} A & \textbf{b} \end{bmatrix} \right)$$ , whereas finding $$A^{- 1}$$ requires about $$2n^{3}$$ flops.
Solving $$L\textbf{y} = \textbf{b}$$ and $$U\textbf{x} = \textbf{y}$$ requires about $$2n^{2}$$ flops, because any $$n \times n$$ triangular system can be solved in about $$n^{2}$$ flops.

Multiplication of $$\textbf{b}$$ by $$A^{- 1}$$ also requires about $$2n^{2}$$ flops, but the result may not be as accurate as that obtained from $$L$$ and $$U$$ (because of roundoff error when computing both $$A^{- 1}$$ and $$A^{- 1}\textbf{b})$$ .﻿

If $$A$$ is sparse (with mostly zero entries), then $$L$$ and $$U$$ may be sparse, too, whereas $$A^{- 1}$$ is likely to be dense. In this case, a solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ with an $$LU$$ factorization is much faster than using $$A^{- 1}$$ . See Exercise 31.

section.heading: A Matrix Factorization in Electrical Engineering
section.paragraph: Matrix factorization is intimately related to the problem of constructing an electrical network with specified properties. The following discussion gives just a glimpse of the connection between factorization and circuit design.

Suppose the box in Figure 3 represents some sort of electric circuit, with an input and output. Record the input voltage and current by $$\begin{bmatrix} v_{1} \\ i_{1} \end{bmatrix}$$ (with voltage $$v$$ in volts and current $$i$$ in amps), and record the output voltage and current by $$\begin{bmatrix} v_{2} \\ i_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$ . Frequently, the transformation $$\begin{bmatrix} v_{1} \\ i_{1} \end{bmatrix}\mapsto\begin{bmatrix} v_{2} \\ i_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$ is linear. That is, there is a matrix $$A$$ , called the transfer matrix, such that
$$\begin{bmatrix} v_{2} \\ i_{2} \end{bmatrix} = A \begin{bmatrix} v_{1} \\ i_{1} \end{bmatrix}$$

image.alt: A circuit diagram shows four wires connecting to a block named an electric circuit. The top two wires are parallel to the bottom two wires.

figure.caption: Figure 3 A circuit with input and output terminals

section.paragraph: Figure 4 shows a ladder network, where two circuits (there could be more) are connected in series, so that the output of one circuit becomes the input of the next circuit. The left circuit in Figure 4 is called a series circuit, with resistance $$R_{1}$$ (in ohms).

image.alt: A circuit diagram shows a series circuit connected in series with a shunt circuit with open circuits on both ends.

section.paragraph: The right circuit in Figure 4 is a shunt circuit, with resistance $$R_{2}$$ . Using Ohm’s law and Kirchhoff’s laws, one can show that the transfer matrices of the series and shunt circuits, respectively, are

$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & - R_{1} \\ 0 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \text{and} & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 0 \\ - 1 / R_{2} & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. \begin{matrix} \text{Transfer} \text{matrix} \\ \text{of} \text{series} \text{circuit} \end{matrix} & & \begin{matrix} \text{Transfer} \text{matrix} \\ \text{of} \text{shunt} \text{circuit} \end{matrix}$$

example.heading: Example 3

list.item: Compute the transfer matrix of the ladder network in Figure 4.
Design a ladder network whose transfer matrix is $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & {- 8} \\ {- .5} & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ .﻿

example.heading: Solution

list.item: Let $$A_{1}$$ and $$A_{2}$$ be the transfer matrices of the series and shunt circuits, respectively. Then an input vector $$\textbf{x}$$ is transformed first into $$A_{1}\textbf{x}$$ and then into $$A_{2}(A_{1}\textbf{x})$$ . The series connection of the circuits corresponds to composition of linear transformations, and the transfer matrix of the ladder network is (note the order)

example.paragraph: $$A_{2} A_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ - 1 / R_{2} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - R_{1} \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - R_{1} \\ - 1 / R_{2} & 1 + R_{1} / R_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$

list.item: To factor the matrix $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & {- 8} \\ {- .5} & 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ into the product of transfer matrices, as in equation (6), look for $$R_{1}$$ and $$R_{2}$$ in Figure 4 to satisfy $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & {- R_{1}} \\ {- 1/R_{2}} & {1 + R_{1}/R_{2}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & {- 8} \\ {- .5} & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ From the $$(1,2) \text{-entries}$$ , $$R_{1} = 8 \text{o} \text{h} \text{m} \text{s}$$ , and from the $$(2,1) \text{-entries}$$ , $$1/R_{2} = .5 \text{o} \text{h} \text{m}$$ and $$R_{2} = 1/.5 = 2 \text{o} \text{h} \text{m} \text{s}$$ . With these values, the network in Figure 4 has the desired transfer matrix.

section.paragraph: A network transfer matrix summarizes the input–output behavior (the design specifications) of the network without reference to the interior circuits. To physically build a network with specified properties, an engineer first determines if such a network can be constructed (or realized). Then the engineer tries to factor the transfer matrix into matrices corresponding to smaller circuits that perhaps are already manufactured and ready for assembly. In the common case of alternating current, the entries in the transfer matrix are usually rational complex-valued functions. (See Exercises 21 and 22 in Section 2.4.) A standard problem is to find a minimal realization that uses the smallest number of electrical components.
